summary:
Trinidad and Tobago's criminal law and its protective framework point in opposite directions. In Jones v Attorney General (2018) the High Court struck down the colonial same-sex criminal provisions, in a challenge brought by activist Jason Jones after he stated publicly that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner; the ruling was upheld on appeal. Decriminalisation removed exposure to prosecution but produced no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no mechanism for changing documents.

Entry rules have not caught up with the criminal-law ruling. Section 8 of the Immigration Act prohibits homosexual men and women who are not citizens from entering Trinidad and Tobago. The provision is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice, ruling on Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson's case, held that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize had violated his freedom of movement, while clarifying that neither state may exclude gay nationals of other CARICOM states under the Treaty of Chaguaramas notwithstanding their domestic laws barring gay entry.

Trans visitors have no route to recognition of their documents or their gender. The director of the TT Transgender Coalition, Rae Alibey, stated in July 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised at all, that gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation, and that institutional forms carry no gender-identity markers. She called for national discussion and attitudinal research as prerequisites for change.

There is no hate-crime category in the legislation. Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne identified that gap in June 2024 in connection with a spate of Grindr-related attacks numbering almost half a dozen in recent months. Police issued a further warning in November 2024 over criminals who create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings ending in armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with two separate incidents reported in a single week.

The constitutional route to protection was closed in 2024. The PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution, with the decision announced at a special convention in August 2024. CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community had 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'.

Family law offers nothing. Trinidad and Tobago does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions; households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible to the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex households; and same-sex couples are unable to adopt. In July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property-dispute resolution between two gay partners, noting the unequal treatment under current law and warning that absent agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to divide property after the dissolution of a same-sex union.

Detention carries a specific and documented risk. The 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018, states plainly that there are no special facilities in the Trinidad and Tobago penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to make recommendations to prison authorities so that provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and it instructs courts to address intersex and transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress. Housing placement for trans prisoners therefore rests on a discretionary sentencing recommendation, with no facility of its own.
tangentialFactors:
Official rhetoric has separated protection from recognition. In June 2016 Prime Minister Keith Rowley told Parliament that the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws. The 2024 constitutional-review exclusion is consistent with that pattern of withholding legal reform while disclaiming hostility.

Public attitudes have been documented as hostile. A 2009 University of the West Indies study for the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed it was justified to deny someone rights or equality on the basis of sexual orientation; the finding prompted the founding of CAISO to press for public discussion and legislative protection.

Some widely circulated descriptions of the country are out of date. A GlobalGayz travel and culture profile from August 2012 states that homosexuality is illegal and that the laws are mostly ignored in practice. That statement of the law predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling and does not reflect current law, although its description of a tourist-facing social scene may still describe how the islands present to visitors.

Visitor-facing risk in the dating and nightlife scene is concentrated rather than diffuse: the documented 2024 attacks and lure-to-robbery incidents cluster on apps rather than on bars or streets, and the absence of a hate-crime category means such incidents are not recorded or charged as bias offences.
localsOnly:
The marginalisation described by the TT Transgender Coalition in July 2024 is a resident condition: the group is not recognised at all, gender identity is not tracked separately from sexual orientation, and forms issued by institutions carry no gender-identity marker. Alibey's call for national discussions and attitudinal research is directed at the domestic policy process.

The Gender Equality Protocol applies to Trinbagonians in the court system. Judicial officers are instructed to use a person's chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress, but the physical-safety provision for prisoners works only through recommendations made at sentencing. There is no standing prison policy or designated facility backing it, so protection depends on which officer sentences the person and on how prison authorities respond.

Civil society for LGBTQ youth operates domestically. The Silver Lining Foundation works to end bullying against LGBTQ youth, and CAISO was founded in the wake of the 2009 UWI study to encourage public discussion and legislative protections.

The constitutional-review exclusion in August 2024 is an internal party process: the PNM Constitution Review Committee's decision to reject sexual-orientation protections, taken at a special convention, forecloses one domestic avenue for statutory change.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Section 8 of the Immigration Act has been applied to any visitor since the 2018 decriminalisation ruling. No source in the inventory records an enforcement, a refusal of entry on that ground, or any court challenge to the section post-Jones; the only enforcement assessment available is that the law is not known to have been enforced.

Unresolved: whether the Caribbean Court of Justice's 2016 clarification on CARICOM free movement has been operationalised in border practice. The ruling's effect on non-CARICOM foreign visitors, as distinct from citizens of regional member states, is not addressed by any source here.

Unresolved: whether any prison housing incident involving a trans inmate has occurred under the 2018 Gender Equality Protocol. The protocol's own statement that no special facilities exist is sourced; no incident reports, complaints or litigation outcomes are available in the inventory.

Unresolved: whether the 2024 Grindr attack cases resulted in charges, convictions or sentences, and whether any were examined as bias-motivated despite the absence of a hate-crime category. The sources record the attacks and the police warnings only.

Not sourced: any post-2024 development in legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination legislation, or a fresh constitutional challenge following Jones. The most recent material in the inventory dates to November 2024 and records no change.
